The Learner Designed major supports the mission of the University by encompassing “Our undergraduate, graduate, and professional education, research, and outreach serve Rhode Island 6

Students, faculty, staff, and alumni are united in one common purpose: to learn and lead together." Because of the broad scope of an interdisciplinary studies degree, graduates holding it are prepared for and able to obtain a variety of jobs.
Students graduating with a Bachelor of Interdisciplinary Studies degree frequently attain and succeed in jobs in one of their fields of study.
The Learner Designed major is closely aligned with the strategic themes and goals of the Academic Plan 2016-2021, particularly with Goal 1: Enhance Student Success: Transform undergraduate and graduate student learning and academic support with a firm commitment to student success and the development of knowledgeable, skilled, and engaged graduates prepared for an ever-changing world.

In Rhode Island, about 54% of adults age 25 and over have completed a high school credential but have not completed a bachelor's degree, accounting for almost four hundred thousand people in the state (Shapiro et. al, 2014).
Some people among this group have completed at least some college credits but did not conplete a collegiate degree (Shapiro et. al, 2014).
Nationally, more than 36 million adults have completed some college credits but have not completed a degree (Higher Ed Insight, 2012).
In Rhode Island, just over 11,000 people have completed at least two years of college level credits without completing a certificate or degree (Shapiro et. al, 2014).
These figures provide an additional source of potential new adult college students or college completer s that may benefit from pursuing a BIS in the Learner Designed major at URI and increase their opportunity for employment or career advancement.
As such, the Learner Designed major also may serve to narrow the growing credentials gap among job seekers without a bachelor's degree and job opportunities that increasingly require this credential (Pew Research Center, 2016).

The Learner Designed major can be used by those in need of undergraduate credentials, but it can also be used as a stepping stone to access a path toward graduate education.

THE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND ALAN SHAWN FEINSTEIN COLLEGE OF EDUCATION AND PROFESSIONAL STUDIES THINKBIG WEDO" SCHOOL OF PROFESSIONAL AND CONTINUING STUDIES Shepard Building,80Washington Street,Providence,RI2903SA 3/16/21 Dear Chris Kincaid and the Curriculum and Standards Committee, I write as a follow-up to our conversation (3/15/21) regarding the Interdisciplinary Studies Learner Designed (Three- Minor) Major proposal submitted by the School of Professional Studies.
Offered below are reflections and rationale for this innovative program.Thank youfor your review.
Sincerely, Jonathan Kroll Program Rationale: The Schoolof Professional Studies is motivated to provide relevant and resonant programs for S.T.A.R. (Service members, Transfer, Adult, and Returning) students.
The vast majority of these students are working full time while studying, caring for family, and serving their communities.
The Learner Designed Major (also referred to as the Three Minor Major)was crafted so that enrolled students can curate a program-of-study that will enable them to acquire knowledge and advance their professional pursuits.

Rather than force these students into traditional academic programs, this major degree combines three minors of the students own choosing,integrates their learning through specific interdisciplinary (BIS) courses, and fulfills General Education and elective credits to reinforce URI's commitment to a comprehensive learning experience.
Q1)What are thegoals and the purposes of students selecting the Three Minor Major?
S.T.A.R. students are unique in that their academic pursuits are directly connected to their professional status and objectives.
They are working full-time.
Many have been for years,if not decades.
The Three Minor Major is structured to maximize the connections between their professional stations and academic coursework.Rather than study in a traditional major program, the learner designed program enables students to immerse themselves in three academic areas-of-attention.For example,if one of our students is a Coordinator of a nonprofit community agency that focuses on food injustice for an elderly population, she might combine the Gerontology, Hunger Studies, and Leadership Studies minors to curate a highly specialized and resonant Major.

No single major degree would be as academically supportive to her current and future professional endeavors as this combination.
Similarly, if a student was the Chef/Owner of a sports bar, he might combine minors in Finance, Marketing, and Sports Mediaand Communication to center his studies on what matters most to him.No singular major can provide an academic course of study that is as preparatory for his particular academic needs and interests than the strategic combination of three minor degrees.
The University of Rhode Island is an equal opportunity employer commited to community equity and diversity and to the principles of a ff rm at ive action.

Q2) Do the minors need to be related or can a student use any 3 minors that the university offers?
Students enrolled in the Three Minor Major can include any three minors of their choosing.
This is intended to provide maximum flexibility while aiso ensuring the design of their major reflects each student's individualized academic and professional pursuits.
Q3) Is there a requirement of a specific number of 300-level courses?
No.
Students are not required to take a specific number of 300-level courses.
Q4) Can you give a quick summary of the program including how the student will be advised?
When students enroll in the Learner Designed Major, they will meet with both their Academic Advisor as well as the School of Professional Studies’ Director.
These initial conversations are intended to lay a foundation and ensure that the students have both the discipline and a clarity of what is expected as Three Minor Major students.
These students will also enroll in BIS 199, the program's introductory course.
Here, they will explore critical approaches to interdisciplinary thinking and begin reflecting on which minors will support their pursuits.

As students continue through their program, they will meet regularly with their Academic Advisor to ensure their course selections strategically align with their intended three minors as well as other requisite courses (i.e., General Education).
Following the completion of at least two courses in each minor, they will enroll in BIs 299a two-credit course designed to assist these students in intentionally integrating their learning. (Students’ Advising conversations will illuminate the desire that this program is intended to be interdisciplinary and that each semester they should be registering for courses in multiple disciplines, rather than attempting to complete one minor one before the others.) Similar to the BIS 199, the BIS 299 course will be taught by a core faculty member within the School of Professional Studies.
Further advising by their formal Academic Advisor and faculty members, will enable these students to strategically select courses that fulfill minor, general education, and elective credits-—-rather than random courses that do not lead to degree fulfillment.
The program concludes with BIS 399: Supervised Senior Project.

With this course, students will be expected to purposefully integrate their multi-discipline learning in a culminating academic project. (This course will also be taught by a core faculty member from the School of Professional Studies.) Similar to all School of Professional Studies students, these Learner Designed Major students will engage in tailored advising conversations throughout their URI experience.
More so, as an intimate community, Academic Advisors, Administrators, and Faculty are constantly engaging with one another as well as in advisory dialogue with students to best be of support, serve as guides, and maximize adult-learner best-practices.
We expect this to continue when the Three Minor Major degree is approved and ultimately launches. 2

Sustainable Food Systems Degree Program and Masters of Environmental Science and Management (M.E.S.M.) Degree Program B.S. in Aquaculture and Fisheries Science Aquaculture and Fisheries play an essential role in the sustainability and health of our planet by providing food and other services.
This major prepares students for professional, technical, academic, or research careers focused on the safe and sustainable production of products and services from aquatic (marine and freshwater) environments.
Core values include an emphasis on the intrinsic value of sustainable food production in the context of other ecosystem processes, heterogeneous scales of production (from small farms and fishers that sell directly to consumers to large scale producers), and preserving local cultures and biodiversity while understanding future demands.

The major requires 10 credits in introductory professional courses including AFS 105G/106, EEC 105, and NRS 100; and a minimum of 24 credits in basic sciences including BIO 101/103, BIO 102/104, CHM 101/102 or CHM 103/105, one course in mathematics (MTH 103, MTH 111, MTH 131 or MTH 141), one course in the physical sciences, one course in ecology or ecosystem science, and one course in computational sciences or statistics.
In addition, the major requires a minimum of 20 credits in concentration courses at the 300 level or above, and 12 credits of the concentration courses must be selected from courses offered by AFS.
The additional credits of the concentration may be selected from courses offered in BIO, EEC, MAF, NRS, and OCG.
The major also requires a minimum of 3 credits in an internship or special project.

A total of 120 credits is required for graduation.

Animal and veterinary sciences play a vital role in the management and care of livestock, companion animals as well as those animals maintained at zoos, aquariums and laboratory animal facilities.
Options are available to students interested in animal sciences or veterinary medicine.

Including the core courses, there are 25-46 credits of basic science including BIO 101/103 and BIO 102/104, 21-31 credits of concentration courses and 11-30 credits of supporting courses required for this major.

Animal Science Option.
This option includes coursework in animal management, nutrition, physiology, behavior, and disease, and provides broad flexibility for students in their choice of animal science courses.
Students have the option to focus their coursework specifically on domestic livestock, exotic animals or animal technology, or be more broadly focused.

7 Research techniques and procedures for animal care are emphasized along with a strong background in the sciences. Students in this option pursue careers as researchers, veterinary technicians, food animal producers, laboratory animal technicians or high school agricultural education teachers. Additionally, there are career opportunities at zoos or aquariums (educator, researcher and exotic animal manager), within the federal, state and local government as well as with many animal-related businesses.

B.S. in Sustainable Agriculture and Food Systems Students completing this interdisciplinary program will graduate with the skills and knowledge needed to contribute to the sustainable development, production, harvesting, management, and utilization of terrestrial and aquatic microorganisms, plants and animals by society worldwide.
The major will allow participants to explore the food chain, from farm to plate to waste and back, emphasizing sustainability, impacts on human health, and resilience from economic, environmental, and societal viewpoints.

Core values of this interdisciplinary program that distinguish it from more traditional agriculture programs include an emphasis on the intrinsic value of heterogeneous scales of production (from small farms that sell directly to consumers to large scale producers), preserving local food cultures and biodiversity while understanding the way other cultures produce and use food (from local to global), using an ecosystem-based approach to agriculture (also integrating the contributions of aquaculture and fisheries), and the greening of urban landscapes.
By the time of degree completion students will be uniquely poised to enter the workforce in the growing field of sustainable food systems or pursue management (through governmental and non- governmental agencies) and graduate education/research opportunities addressing the challenges of securing access to safe and affordable food for a growing population.

SAFS students will pursue a curriculum that combines depth in a specialization area chosen from three options within the program (Sustainable Agriculture, Nutrition and Food, and Food and Society) with breadth across the natural and social sciences, engineering, and the arts and humanities.

10 Sustainable Agriculture Option: Students in this option will specialize in the harvesting and production of either terrestrial or aquatic plants and animals for human uses.

The M.E.S.M. degree program serves graduate students from six departments within URI’s College of Environment and Life Sciences (CELS): Environmental and Natural Resource Economics; Fisheries, Animal and Veterinary Science; Geosciences; Marine Affairs; Natural Resources Science; and Plant Sciences.

The M.E.S.M. degree program has the following Specializations: Conservation biology; earth and hydrologic science; environmental communication; environmental planning and design; environmental policy and management; remote sensing and spatial analysis; sustainable systems; and wetland, watershed, and ecosystem science.
